title: Volume and surface area of pyramid, cone and sphere
summary: Distinguish perpendicular height, slant height and radius, then calculate volumes and exposed surface areas of pyramids, cones, spheres and composite solids.
objectives: Choose the correct dimensions and formula for a pyramid, cone or sphere.
Calculate volume, curved surface area and total exposed surface area.
Solve reverse and composite-solid problems with consistent units and suitable rounding.

sections.title: Read the solid before choosing a formula

blocks.text: Mensuration questions often provide several lengths, but each formula uses particular dimensions. The radius runs from the centre of a circular base to its edge, so it is half the diameter. A perpendicular height meets the base at 90° and is used in every volume formula. A slant height lies on a triangular or curved face and is used for surface area.

Volume measures space inside a solid and uses cubic units. Surface area measures the exposed covering and uses square units. Sketch the solid, label r, h and l, and decide whether the question asks for inside space, curved covering, or every exposed face before substituting.

sections.title: Pyramids: one third of the matching prism

blocks.text: A pyramid has a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at an apex. Its volume is one third of the volume of a prism with the same base area and perpendicular height. For surface area, calculate the base and each triangular face separately. A triangular face area uses the perpendicular height within that face, which is usually a slant height rather than the pyramid’s vertical height.

sections.title: Worked example: square-based pyramid

prompt.text: A square-based pyramid has base side 10 cm, perpendicular height 12 cm and slant height 13 cm on every triangular face. Find its volume and total surface area.

content.text: The base area is 10² = 100 cm². Use the perpendicular height for volume.
Each triangular face has area ½ × 10 × 13 = 65 cm². There are four equal faces.

sections.verification_note: The volume is one third of the 1,200 cm³ matching prism, and the surface area includes exactly one base plus four triangular faces.

sections.title: Cones: keep vertical and slant height separate

blocks.text: A cone is one third of the matching cylinder, so its volume uses the vertical height h. Its curved surface unwraps to a sector and has area πrl, where l is the slant height. Add the circular base πr² only when the base is exposed. In a right cone, r, h and l form a right triangle, so l² = r² + h².

sections.title: Worked example: find a cone’s slant height first

prompt.text: A closed cone has radius 5 cm and perpendicular height 12 cm. Find its volume and total surface area, giving answers to 1 decimal place.

content.text: Use the right triangle through the centre to find the slant height.
The cone is closed, so include curved area and its base.

sections.verification_note: The slant height 13 cm is longer than both perpendicular sides, and the total area exceeds the curved area 65π cm².

blocks.text: Every point on a sphere is the same distance r from its centre. The volume formula contains r³, while surface area contains r², so confusing radius with diameter causes a large error. A hemisphere has half the sphere’s volume and half its curved area. Its total surface area also includes the flat circular base.

sections.title: Worked example: hemisphere container

prompt.text: An open hemispherical bowl has internal diameter 18 cm. Find its capacity and the curved internal area, giving answers to 1 decimal place.

content.text: The radius is 9 cm. Capacity is the hemisphere’s internal volume.
The bowl is open, so no flat circular base is included.

sections.verification_note: The hemisphere’s results are half the corresponding sphere results, and the radius used is half the stated diameter.

blocks.text: For a composite solid, add volumes of joined pieces and subtract volumes of holes or removed pieces. For surface area, count only surfaces exposed to air, liquid, paint or wrapping. A circular join between a cone and hemisphere is internal, so it is excluded from the outside area. Write a short surface inventory before calculating.

Convert all lengths to one unit before using formulas. Since 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m² = 10,000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³. Keep π and unrounded intermediate values on the calculator, then round once at the end and attach the correct square or cubic unit.

prompt.text: A sphere has diameter 12 cm. Enter its surface area as a multiple of π; for example, enter 20 for 20π.

feedback.text: The radius is 6 cm, so 4πr² = 4π(6²) = 144π cm².

blocks.text: Mark radius versus diameter and vertical height versus slant height. Choose volume or surface area, list the exposed faces, and convert lengths before substituting.

Use cubic units for volume and square units for area. Retain π and full calculator precision until the final line, round only as requested, and check that a one-third or one-half factor has not been missed.
